input: It is important to note that the proposed schedule float of 14% for the upgrade project has been the subject of some discussion, particularly in relation to the possibility that a lower alternative might be adopted instead. While a reduced figure could appear attractive at first sight, it would nevertheless leave the programme with considerably less room to respond when an approval, a delivery, or an interface between different packages takes longer than the planned sequence allows. The steering group is therefore not being asked to view the float simply as spare time that happens to sit at the end of the programme. Rather, the float should be understood as a mechanism for protecting the order of the work, in the sense that a delay arising in one package can be absorbed before it is passed on to the next package and effectively converted into a change in the completion position. This is especially relevant where dependencies cannot be run in parallel and where a late input can hold up more than the package that formally owns that input. It should also be emphasised that reducing the float would not, in itself, remove those dependencies. The figure of 14% should accordingly be read alongside the cost position for the upgrade project, with reference to the cost table in the Costs section, whose figures are not repeated here.
target: The case for holding the schedule float at 14% for the upgrade project rests on the work the float has to cover. A lower alternative would leave the programme with less room when an approval, a delivery, or an interface between packages takes longer than the sequence allows. The steering group is not being asked to treat the float as spare time at the end of the programme. The float protects the order of the work: a delay in one package is absorbed before the delay is passed to the next package and converted into a change to the completion position. That protection matters most where the programme has dependencies that cannot be run in parallel and where a late input stops more than the package that owns the input. Removing part of the float would not remove those dependencies. The figure also has to be read with the cost position for the upgrade project. The excerpt refers to the cost table in the Costs section and does not repeat its figures; the schedule argument stands on the stated percentage and on the sequence risk it covers. A smaller allowance would be defensible only if the sequence had fewer hard dependencies or if the steering group accepted a weaker completion position as the price of the reduction. Neither change is made in the excerpt. The defence is therefore narrow: the percentage is retained because the dependencies remain, and because the cost discussion is kept in the Costs section rather than mixed into the schedule allowance. For the steering group, the choice is between retaining 14% as the programme allowance and accepting that a smaller allowance transfers ordinary slippage directly to the end date.
